rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tubba‘ refers to Yemen’s Tabābi‘ah, renowned in Arabia for material power, advancement, and intellectual ability; Arab poets praised them extensively.
rows.anchor: Tabā bi‘ah of Yemen who were very famous in Arabia because of their material might and advancement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh are challenged to explain their arrogance: if even the mightier Tubba‘ were destroyed, what makes them think no one can seize them?
rows.anchor: the Qur’ ān has asked them to speak up if they are superior to the nation of the Tubba‘

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ‘Ād, Thamūd, and other earlier peoples surpassed Quraysh in every respect, yet God destroyed them when they rebelled.
rows.anchor: The people of the ‘ Ād, the Tham ūd and some other nations were superior to the Quraysh in every respect

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God values character and morality over wealth or military power; morally corrupt nations can be destroyed by the weapons they made, effectively committing suicide with them.
rows.anchor: What counts for God is character and morality and not material wealth and riches nor grand mansions nor atom bombs and missiles.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abundant worldly examples of retribution make it unreasonable to doubt a final day when individuals receive the kind of reward or punishment nations have received.
rows.anchor: Examples of God’s law of retribution are found in this world and are found so abundantly that they are uncountable.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The argument now moves from historical and worldly evidence to God’s attributes and their moral and intellectual implications.
rows.anchor: argument for the same is drawn from the attributes of God and from what they morally and intellectually entail.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God created the heavens, earth, and what lies between them for a true, higher purpose; that purpose requires the world to end and a day of reward and punishment to follow.
rows.anchor: It is an essential requirement of this true objective that one day this world cease to exist and after that a day come

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A world without judgment would make its wise and merciful Creator seem like a spectator who ends an injustice-filled drama from boredom or leaves it running forever; this is an untenable notion, though widespread.
rows.anchor: Obviously, this notion is such a wrong estimation about the merciful and wise creator of this world that cannot even be imagined.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The purposeful creation of the world entails an appointed judgment day: God’s knowledge, justice, wisdom, and mercy require that He decide everyone’s affairs and reward upright people and punish transgressors.
rows.anchor: it is against the knowledge, justice, wisdom and mercy of God that this world continues the way it is or ends abruptly

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphasized word all underscores that no one escapes perfect justice: people of every rank are summoned, realities stay hidden from none, and no one can obstruct judgment.
rows.anchor: The small and the big, the rulers and the ruled, the beggar and the king – all will be called to justice

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mawlā denotes blood-related family or tribal kin with mutual feelings of support and unity; on that day no such relative can benefit another.
rows.anchor: members of a family and tribe who are related to a person through his blood and lineage

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse’s denial of help also rules out other aid; in context, it is the assistance Arab idolaters expected from their deities.
rows.anchor: It is evident from contextual indication that this help refers to the help which the Idolaters of Arabia expected from their deities.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only those granted God’s mercy succeed, and those receiving it are worthy of it; God is both powerful and merciful.
rows.anchor: only those who are blessed with God’s grace will succeed and only those receive His grace who are worthy of it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No one can bail out people seized by God.
rows.anchor: No one will be able to bail out people seized by

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zaqqūm is the sinners’ food in Hell; its reality is known only to God, and people can only imagine it vaguely by analogy with earthly cactus.
rows.anchor: We can only vaguely imagine it by drawing an analogy from the cactus of this world.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Among varying translations of muhl, Islahi prefers sediment of oil, following the word’s etymological construction.
rows.anchor: By giving preference to its etymological construction, I have translated it as the sediment of oil.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The simile combines the heat and bitterness of boiling oil sediment, which does not sizzle, with the sizzling of heated water.
rows.anchor: Here in this simile both facets of heating are combined.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For eloquence, the source of the pronouncement is left unstated; the command itself is given, with Hell’s wardens directed to seize and drag the sinner deep into Hell and pour boiling water over him.
rows.anchor: Giving due consideration to eloquence, it is suppressed that the above words will be proclaimed to these people from God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wardens are ordered to seize the sinner, drag him to Hell’s depth, and pour boiling water over his head as punishment.
rows.anchor: wardens of Hell will be directed to seize these people and drag them to the depth of Hell

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The taunt can be read as an expression of the punishment and situation that now befall the sinner, rather than as speech by an identified speaker.
rows.anchor: This statement can be an expression of the situation that will befall these people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the taunt may be spoken by Hell’s wardens.
rows.anchor: it can also be interpreted to be made by the wardens.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sinners who once posed as powerful and honourable, arrogantly denied the Day, and doubted it are told to taste the very torment they questioned.
rows.anchor: they posed to be very powerful and honourable in the previous world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The God-fearing dwell in a peaceful place among gardens and fountains, free from fear and sorrow.
rows.anchor: After depicting the fate of the sinners, the verses portray the fate of the God-fearing: they will reside in a peaceful place

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They need not fear that their blessings will be taken away, end, or become grounds for accountability.
rows.anchor: they will have no fear that anyone snatch away these blessings from them or that the blessings cease

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sundus and istabraq are names for silk cloth.
rows.anchor: are the names of silk cloth.

rows.speaker: Some people
rows.claim: Some people distinguish sundus from istabraq by the fabrics’ thickness.
rows.anchor: Some people have distinguished between them with regard to their thickness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The thickness distinction is immaterial for garments of Paradise; only God knows what these fabrics will actually be like.
rows.anchor: since these fabrics belong to Paradise, such a distinction is unimportant. Only God knows what actually they will be like.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mutaqābilīn means that the people will face one another.
rows.anchor: here refers to the fact that these people will face one another.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The syntax implies verbs such as sitting or reclining, which are understood but not expressed.
rows.anchor: will be considered as understood to be present here.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Facing each other signifies affection and mutual trust, a fitting recompense for the noble counsel they gave one another in worldly life.
rows.anchor: Sitting facing one another shows that they will be dear to one another and will enjoy the confidence of one another.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In contrast, disbelievers and their leaders will hurl insults at one another.
rows.anchor: the disbelievers and their leaders will hurl insults at each other.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their bliss culminates in marriage to large-eyed houris; in Arabic literature, the epithet denotes the pinnacle of a woman’s beauty.
rows.anchor: In Arabic literature, this epithet signifies the pinnacle of beauty of a woman.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They will have abundant fruit of every kind and request whatever they desire from dutiful attendants.
rows.anchor: Whatever fruit they want, they will demand from dutiful attendants.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fruit will not diminish or be withheld, and they will have no fear of death; they are shielded from every fear and enjoy eternal bliss.
rows.anchor: They will be shielded from all fears and enjoy eternal bliss.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word first means their worldly death is the only death they will taste; their life and pleasure thereafter are abiding.
rows.anchor: after the death they tasted in this world, they will never taste it again

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their Lord frees them from death and Hell; this special divine favour is the supreme triumph.
rows.anchor: This is a special favour to them by the Prophet’s Lord, and this, in reality, is the supreme triumph

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: True success differs from worldly people’s fixation on this life as the only existence, with no life or death beyond it.
rows.anchor: the slaves of this world have given their hearts to and have been so infatuated with their love

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah closes by returning to its opening theme: the Qur’an’s exaltedness as a great favour to the Arabs, whose valuation of it brings success while arrogance brings destruction; the intervening argument established its truth.
rows.anchor: sūrah began with the mention of the Qur’ ān’s exaltedness: it is indeed a great favour which the Almighty has blessed the Arabs with.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Like examples in earlier sūrahs, an eloquent orator closes by recalling the opening topic, giving the audience a complete final reminder.
rows.anchor: An orator generally ends his speech by reminding the audience of the topic with which he began it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening particle fa connects this verse with the subject of the preceding sections.
rows.anchor: The letter فindicates the affinity with the subject of the previous sections
